title: Not yet ripe
hookLine: Meghiya insists on going alone and is overwhelmed; five things ripen the mind

lines: A MANGO GROVE BY THE RIVER.
cards: Meghiya is serving as the Buddha's attendant. One morning, coming back from alms in a village, he walks along a river and finds a mango grove so lovely he can hardly stand it. Quiet, shady, by the water.
The perfect place to meditate, he thinks. He hurries back and asks permission to go and sit there. Wait, the Buddha says.
We're alone here. Stay until another monk comes. Meghiya asks again.
Wait. A third time. And this time the Buddha says: what can I say, when you speak of striving?

teach.h: THE PERFECT PLACE, A RESTLESS MIND.
teach.b: Meghiya goes and sits under a mango tree in the perfect grove. And there, in the perfect place, his mind is overrun.
Three kinds of thought keep coming at him: thoughts of sense-pleasure, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harming. He's amazed: I went forth out of faith, and here I am, swarmed by these.
He comes back and tells the Buddha everything.
The Buddha doesn't say I told you so.
He says that when the mind's release is not yet ripe, five things bring it to ripeness.
First, a good friend, a good companion. Second, keeping the training, living with integrity. Third, talk that actually helps: about wanting little, contentment, solitude, energy, wisdom.
Fourth, effort, letting go of what's unskillful and taking up what's skillful. Fifth, wisdom that sees how things rise and pass. And notice which comes first.
The good friend: the very thing Meghiya walked away from when he left the Buddha alone to sit in his beautiful grove.

Then the Buddha adds what to do with the thoughts: reflect on the body's unattractiveness to ease lust, kindness to ease ill will, mindfulness of breathing to cut the chatter, and seeing impermanence to uproot the conceit I am.
The place wasn't the problem. Meghiya wasn't ready yet, and the Buddha could see it. Ripeness can't be rushed.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the Meghiya Sutta to explain why practice is done with a teacher and a community, and the five supports it lists are taught across Theravada monastic life.

o: a good friend who helps you grow
a quiet place, perfect for meditation
a teacher you must obey in all things

games.q: not yet ripe: tap the pairs.
p: the attendant who wanted to go
the perfect place, a restless mind

s: the Buddha let Meghiya go the first time he asked
he asked him to wait until another monk came; Meghiya asked three times.
in the perfect grove, Meghiya's mind was overrun by three kinds of thought
a good friend is the first of the five things that ripen the mind
the list begins with admirable friendship.

games.q: you're the Buddha. your attendant comes back from his perfect grove, overwhelmed by thoughts. what do you do?
o: remind him you told him to wait.
teach him five things that ripen the mind.
send him back to try harder.
games.why: no reproach. he teaches the five supports, starting with a good friend, and how to meet each kind of thought.

practice: Bring to mind one piece of advice you've been given lately and brushed aside, from a parent, a friend, a doctor, a teacher.

Let yourself hear it again without defending against it, and ask whether there's something here you're not ripe enough to see yet. You don't have to decide anything; just let it be heard, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kalyanamitta, a good friend. Meghiya rushed to a perfect grove and was overwhelmed; the Buddha named five things that ripen the mind, starting with this.

orig.note: Pali kalyanamitta: a good, admirable friend, the first of the five things in Udana 4.1.

carryVoice: Your line: a good friend comes first. Even the perfect grove can wait for that. Day six hundred eighteen, complete.
